topic.name: The Shell Method: Rotation About the Y-Axis

question.text: Consider the finite region bounded between the curves $y=x$ and $y=x^2-2x.$ Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis.
question.explanation:
First, let $f(x)=x$ and $g(x)=x^2-2x.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f(x) &= g(x) \\[3pt] x &= x^2-2x \\[3pt] x^2- 3x &= 0 \\[3pt] x \left(x - 3 \right) &= 0 \end{align*}

The solutions are $x=0$ and $x=3.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=3.$

Now, let's draw our usual vertical arrow through the region to determine the lower and upper functions.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the lower function $y=g(x)=x^2-2x,$ and

  • leaves through the upper function $y=f(x)=x.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

\begin{align*} V &= 2\pi \int_{a}^{b} x \big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{upper}} \big] - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{lower}} \big] \big) \:\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{3} x \left( [{\color{brown}x}] - [{\color{blue}x^2-2x}] \right) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = 2\pi \int_0^3 x(3x-x^2) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = 2\pi \int_0^3 \left( 3x^2-x^3 \right) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = 2\pi \left. \left(x^3 - \dfrac{x^4}{4} \right) \right|_0^3 \\[5pt] & = 2\pi \left[ \left(27 - \dfrac{81}{4} \right) - 0 \right] \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {27\pi}{2} \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Volume of a Solid When a Region is Enclosed Between Two Curves

question.text: Consider the finite region bounded by the curve $y=-6+8x-2x^2$ and the $x$-axis, shown above. What integral gives the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis?
question.explanation:
First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation for $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} -6+8x-2x^2 &= 0 \\[5pt] x^2-4x+3 &= 0 \\[5pt] (x-3)(x-1) &= 0 \\[5pt] \end{align*}

The solutions are $x=1$ and $x=3.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=1$ to $x=3.$

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

\begin{align*} V &= 2\pi \int_{a}^{b} x\, f(x) \:\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{1}^{3} x \left( -6+8x-2x^2 \right) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{1}^{3} \left( -6x+8x^2-2x^3 \right) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 4\pi \int_{1}^{3} \left( -3x+4x^2-x^3 \right) \textrm{d}x \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Volume of a Solid Using the Shell Method

question.text: Consider the finite region bounded between the curves $y=2\sqrt{x}$ and $y=x.$ Calculate the volume $V$ of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
First, let $f(x)=2\sqrt{x}$ and $g(x)=x.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f(x) &= g(x) \\[5pt] 2\sqrt{x} &= x \\[5pt] 4x &= x^2 \\[5pt] x^2-4x &= 0 \end{align*}

The solutions are $x=0$ and $x=4.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=4.$

Now, let's draw our usual vertical arrow through the region to determine the lower and upper functions.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the lower function $y=g(x)=x,$ and

  • leaves through the upper function $y=f(x)=2\sqrt{x}.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

\begin{align*} V &= 2\pi \int_{a}^{b} x \big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{upper}} \big] - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{lower}} \big] \big) \:\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{4} x \left( [{\color{brown}2\sqrt{x}}] - [{\color{blue}x}] \right) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = 2\pi \int_0^4 x(2\sqrt{x}-x) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = 2\pi \int_0^4 \left( 2x^{3/2}-x^2 \right) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = 2\pi \left. \left(\dfrac{4}{5}x^{5/2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3} \right) \right|_0^4 \\[5pt] & = 2\pi \left[ \left(\dfrac{128}{5}- \dfrac{64}{3}\right) - 0 \right] \\[5pt] & = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{128\pi}{15}} \end{align*}
